footer: STRIVE · SKL-3 · Apply the correct Level of Information Need to geometric outputs · schematk.

blocks.text: Over-modelling wastes days and bloats the file. Under-modelling fails the deliverable. Level of Information Need (LOIN) is how you hit the middle — modelling to exactly what the milestone requires, no more, no less.
By the end you'll be able to match geometric detail to a milestone and explain why "more detail" is often the wrong answer.

sections.h2: Detail is a cost, not a virtue

blocks.text: New modellers assume more detail is always better. It isn't. Every extra parameter, every modelled bolt, every fillet costs time to build, slows the model, and can imply a certainty the design doesn't yet have. A concept-stage wall modelled to fabrication detail is misleading, not impressive.

LOIN (from the ISO 19650 world) defines how much information an object needs at a given point, for a given purpose. It has parts — geometry, alphanumeric data, and documentation — but at this level the key idea is simple: the required detail is set by the milestone and the use, not by how much you could model.
LOIN = Level of Information Need. The right amount of information for a specific deliverable and decision. It replaces older, vaguer "LOD" levels with a needs-based test.
blocks.label: Term

blocks.text: Two failure modes sit on either side of "just right." Over-modelling: adding detail the milestone doesn't need — fabrication geometry at concept stage, every screw modelled when a placeholder would do. Under-modelling: too little to support the decision — a coordination model missing the clearances a clash check depends on.
Both are errors against the LOIN. The skill is reading the requirement and stopping at it — delivering a model that's fit for the milestone's purpose and no heavier than it needs to be.

Tap each scenario and decide which ones show the object modelled at the correct LOIN for its stated purpose. The right answers share a logic: the detail matches what the milestone actually needs to decide.

cases.why: ✓ Right-sized. At concept the purpose is spatial coordination — a correctly-dimensioned box answers it. Pipework detail would be premature.
cases.title: Concept stage: a chiller shown as a simple sized box

cases.why: ✗ Over-modelled. Fabrication geometry at concept wastes effort and implies a certainty that doesn't exist yet.
cases.title: Concept stage: every bolt and weld on a steel connection modelled

cases.why: ✓ Right-sized. The purpose is clash detection, so real dimensions and clearances are exactly what's needed — and enough.
cases.title: Coordination model: ductwork with correct size and insulation clearance

cases.why: ✗ Under-modelled. Handover needs asset data; geometry alone fails the purpose. LOIN covers data, not just shape.
cases.desc: Missing the data the milestone needs.
cases.title: Handover model: doors with no fire rating or manufacturer data

config.hintDone: ✓ Both found. Correct LOIN always traces back to the milestone's purpose — model to the decision, not to the maximum.

questions.q: A colleague spends two days modelling every fixing on a handrail for a concept design review. What's the issue?

options.text: Nothing — more detail is always safer
They've over-modelled: the detail exceeds what the concept milestone needs
They've under-modelled and need even more detail

questions.noFeedback: Reconsider — fabrication-level fixings at concept stage is over-modelling. The detail exceeds what the milestone needs to decide.
questions.okFeedback: ✓ Right. Concept review needs intent and arrangement, not fixings. That's effort spent above the required LOIN — time lost and false precision added.

items: LOIN = the right amount of information for a specific milestone and purpose — not the maximum you could produce.
Detail is a cost: it takes time, slows the model, and can imply false certainty.
Over-modelling and under-modelling are both LOIN errors — fit the deliverable's actual need.
LOIN covers geometry and data — a handover model can be geometrically fine but still under-spec on information.
